title: What the Database Does
intro: If you write SQL that works but have never looked at what the engine does with it, this is the layer underneath. Everything here runs in sqlite3 — one binary, no server — so the whole track fits on whatever machine you happen to have open.

days.title: A table is a file of pages
days.teaser: Why reading one row costs four kilobytes, and the hidden column you already have
days.teachBack: A page is the unit of I/O. Explain what that means for a query that returns a single narrow row from a large table — what does the engine actually read, and what would have to be true for it to read less?
days.theoryMarkdown:
You already write queries that work. This track is about the layer underneath them: what
the engine does with the bytes once your `SELECT` arrives. Start with the most physical
question there is — where does a row actually live?

### A row is not the unit of anything

The mental model most people carry is that a table is a list of rows, and reading a row
reads a row. Neither half is true.

A database file is a flat array of fixed-size **pages**. Every page is the same size,
and the page is the unit the engine reads, writes, caches and locks. Rows are packed
into pages; a page holds as many as fit. When you ask for one row, the engine reads the
whole page that row sits in — because that is the smallest thing it can read.

In SQLite the page size is baked into the file at creation:

```sql
PRAGMA page_size;
PRAGMA page_count;
SELECT page_size * page_count AS bytes FROM pragma_page_size(), pragma_page_count();
```

4096 bytes by default, which is not a coincidence: it matches the page size of the
virtual-memory system and of most filesystems, so one database page is one filesystem
page is one memory page. PostgreSQL uses 8192 for the same family of reasons. The
number is a compromise nobody has wanted to relitigate since the 1990s: bigger pages
waste less space on per-page bookkeeping and read more useful bytes per seek, smaller
pages waste less I/O when you only wanted one row.

You can watch the file grow in page-sized steps rather than row-sized ones:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, note TEXT);
PRAGMA page_count;
INSERT INTO t(name, note) VALUES ('a', 'x');
PRAGMA page_count;
```

Creating the table alone takes an empty file to two pages — one for the schema, one for
the table's own root — before a single row exists. Then the first row costs nothing
extra, and neither do the next hundred: the count sits still until a page fills, and the
file gains exactly one more. Growth is in page-sized steps, and the steps have nothing
to do with how many rows you inserted.

### What the row itself is

Inside the page, a row is a length-prefixed run of bytes: a header saying what type each
column is and how long it is, then the values end to end. There is no fixed column
offset to jump to — to read the fourth column the engine walks the first three.

That is why `SELECT *` is not free even when you were going to read most of it, and why
narrow tables are faster than wide ones in ways that surprise people: the cost is not
"per column you asked for", it is "per byte the engine had to walk past".

> [!NOTE]
> This is a **row store**, and it is one of two answers. Column stores — ClickHouse,
> DuckDB, Parquet — put all of one column's values together instead, so a query touching
> three columns of a hundred reads three columns' worth of bytes. That is the whole
> reason analytics engines exist as separate products: same SQL, opposite physical
> layout. Row stores win when you want whole rows; column stores win when you want whole
> columns.

### The hidden column you already have

Every ordinary SQLite table has a `rowid`: a 64-bit integer key that the table is
physically sorted by, whether you asked for one or not.

```sql
SELECT rowid, * FROM t LIMIT 3;
```

That works on a table where no such column was declared. The table is not a heap of rows
in insertion order — it is a B-tree keyed on `rowid`, and "the table" *is* that tree.

Declaring `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` does something special here: it doesn't create a
second key, it makes your column *be* the `rowid`. Exactly that spelling, too —
`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` aliases the rowid, while `INT PRIMARY KEY` or
`BIGINT PRIMARY KEY` do not, and quietly get you a separate index instead. It's the
sharpest edge in SQLite's type system and it is invisible until you measure.

PostgreSQL made the opposite choice: its tables really are unordered heaps, and its
equivalent of a rowid — `ctid` — is a physical address of the form `(page, slot)` that
changes when the row is updated. Two engines, two answers, and knowing which one you're
on changes what "the table's order" even means.

> [!NOTE]
> There is no such thing as the natural order of a table. A `SELECT` with no `ORDER BY`
> may come back in insertion order today and in a different order tomorrow because
> someone added an index, and both are correct. Every "the rows came out shuffled" bug
> is this.

### Worth knowing: the file will tell you about itself

SQLite ships a virtual table called `dbstat` that reports where every page went:

```sql
SELECT name, count(*) AS pages, sum(payload) AS bytes
FROM dbstat
GROUP BY name
ORDER BY pages DESC;
```

One row per table and index, with the page count each is actually costing you. It's the
quickest way to find out that an index you forgot about is twice the size of the table
it indexes.

quiz.prompt: A table has 200 rows packed into 6 pages. You run a query that returns exactly one row, found by scanning. What is the smallest amount of data the engine could have read from disk?

options.text: It depends entirely on the row's width
options.why: Row width changes how many rows fit in a page, and a very wide value can spill onto overflow pages — but the floor is still one page, whatever the row weighs.

options.text: One page — 4KB by default
options.why: The page is the unit of I/O. Even a single-byte column in a single row costs one whole page, because a page is the smallest thing the engine can ask the filesystem for.

options.text: All 6 pages, since a scan reads the whole table
options.why: A scan *may* read every page, but it can stop the moment it has what it needs. The question asks for the smallest possible, and that's the page the row is on.

options.text: Just the bytes of that row
options.why: Nothing in the stack can read a partial page. The row's bytes come along inside the page that holds them; you never pay per row.

quiz.prompt: Why is reading the tenth column of a row more expensive than reading the first, in a row-store engine?

options.text: Columns are stored end to end with no fixed offsets, so reaching the tenth means walking past the first nine
options.why: The row header gives each value's type and length, not its address. Finding column ten is a walk, not a jump — which is why the cost scales with bytes skipped rather than columns requested.

options.text: It isn't — column access is constant time either way
options.why: That would be true if rows were fixed-width C structs with known offsets. They aren't: values are variable-length, so the offsets can't be known in advance.

options.text: The engine has to re-parse the row for each column accessed
options.why: It parses the header once. The cost is the walk through the values, not repeated parsing.

options.text: Later columns are stored on separate overflow pages
options.why: Overflow pages exist, but they're for values too large for a page — a long TEXT or BLOB. Ordinary columns all live in the same row, whatever their position.

quiz.prompt: You declare `id INT PRIMARY KEY` in SQLite instead of `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`. What actually changes?

options.text: Nothing — `INT` and `INTEGER` are synonyms everywhere in SQLite
options.why: They're synonyms for type affinity, which is why this is so easy to miss. For the rowid alias specifically, only the literal word `INTEGER` counts.

options.text: `INT` limits the column to 32 bits
options.why: SQLite stores integers in as many bytes as the value needs, up to 64 bits, regardless of the declared type name.

options.text: `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` makes your column the rowid itself; `INT PRIMARY KEY` leaves the rowid alone and adds a separate index
options.why: Exactly that spelling is load-bearing. One gives you a column that *is* the table's B-tree key; the other gives you a hidden rowid plus an index you pay for on every write.

options.text: `INT PRIMARY KEY` is rejected as a syntax error
options.why: It's perfectly valid, which is the problem — you get a working table with an extra index and no warning that you meant something else.

quiz.prompt: A colleague says "the rows come back in the order I inserted them, I checked." What is wrong with relying on that?

options.text: Without `ORDER BY` the engine may return rows in any order, and adding an index later can silently change it
options.why: Order with no `ORDER BY` is an accident of the plan the optimiser picked today. A new index gives it a cheaper path, the order changes, and nothing was "broken" — the query never asked for an order.

options.text: Insertion order is never preserved, so the observation must be wrong
options.why: The observation is usually right, which is what makes it dangerous. A rowid table scanned in key order really does come back in insertion order — until the plan changes.

options.text: It's fine as long as nobody deletes rows
options.why: Deletes free slots that later inserts can reuse, so they're one way to see it break — but a new index or a different plan will do it without a single delete.

options.text: It only holds if the table has a primary key
options.why: It has nothing to do with declaring a key. Any table can be read by any plan the optimiser prefers.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference in physical layout between a row store and a column store, and which suits `SELECT avg(price) FROM sales` over 50 million rows?

options.text: A row store suits it better, since all the values are already in one place
options.why: "One place" means one *row*. The query wants one column across all rows, which in a row store is the maximally scattered access pattern.

options.text: They're the same on disk and differ only in the query planner
options.why: The layout is the whole difference, and it's why they ship as separate products rather than as a planner flag.

options.text: A column store keeps the same layout but adds an index per column, so it suits the query
options.why: It isn't an index — it's a different physical arrangement of the data itself. There's no row to index into.

options.text: A row store keeps a row's columns together; a column store keeps a column's values together — so the column store reads only `price`
options.why: The aggregate touches one column of the table. A row store must walk every row's bytes to reach it; a column store reads that column's values contiguously and skips the rest of the table entirely.

task.markdown:
Get a database in front of you and look at its pages.

1. Install `sqlite3` if you don't have it — one binary, no server, no configuration. It's
   almost certainly already on your machine.
2. Create a database with one table, insert a few hundred rows, and watch
   `PRAGMA page_count` change as you go. Note where it jumps and where it doesn't.
3. Work out the file's size from `page_size * page_count`, then check it against what
   the filesystem says with `ls -l`. They should agree.
4. Select `rowid` from your table even though you never declared it.
5. Then query `dbstat` and find out how many pages your table is actually costing.
checklist: observed `page_count` jumping in steps rather than growing per row
`page_size * page_count` checked against the real file size on disk
selected `rowid` from a table that never declared it
`dbstat` queried for the per-table page count

days.title: An index is a sorted copy
days.teaser: Your index exists, the column is right, and the plan still says SCAN. Three reasons why.
days.teachBack: An index is a second sorted tree, not an annotation. Use that to explain both why `WHERE lower(email) = ?` can't use an index on `email`, and why the fix is an index on the expression rather than on the column.
days.theoryMarkdown:
Yesterday: a table is pages, and finding a row without help means reading them all.
Today: what an index actually is, and the exact reasons a perfectly good one gets
ignored.

### It is a second table you don't get to see

An index is not an annotation on a table, and it is not a hint. It is **another B-tree,
containing the indexed columns plus a pointer back to the row**, kept sorted.

That single sentence explains almost everything indexes do:

- Lookups get fast because the tree is sorted, so finding a value is a descent through
  a handful of pages instead of a walk through all of them.
- Writes get slower because every `INSERT` now writes two trees, and every `UPDATE` of
  an indexed column writes two trees.
- The database gets bigger, sometimes larger than the table, because the index is a
  real copy of real data.
- `ORDER BY` on the indexed column can become free — the sorted order already exists on
  disk, so there is nothing to sort.

You never pay for an index once. You pay on every write, forever, in exchange for the
reads.

### Ask the engine what it plans to do

Never guess about this. Every engine will tell you, and in SQLite the question is:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, note TEXT);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = 'name7';
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON t(name);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = 'name7';
```

Before the index, the plan is one word you should learn to dread:

```
SCAN t
```

After it:

```
SEARCH t USING INDEX idx_name (name=?)
```

(`SELECT *` here wants `note`, which the index doesn't carry — hold that thought.)

**SCAN means every row. SEARCH means a descent.** In PostgreSQL the same distinction is
`Seq Scan` versus `Index Scan`, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` there will also run the query and
report what really happened, which is the version you want when the estimate and reality
disagree.

### Why a perfectly good index gets ignored

Here is the rule that catches everyone: **an index on a column can only answer questions
about that column's value.** The moment you wrap the column in a function, you are
asking about a different value, and the sorted copy is sorted by the wrong thing.

```sql
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM t WHERE lower(name) = 'name7';
```

`SCAN t`, with `idx_name` sitting right there. The index is ordered by `name`; the query
asks about `lower(name)`; nothing in the tree is in that order. Same story for
`WHERE price * 1.2 > 100`, `WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-01-01'`, and every
`WHERE CAST(id AS TEXT) = ?` written to make a type error go away.

The fix is to index the expression you actually query:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_lower ON t(lower(name));
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM t WHERE lower(name) = 'name7';
```

```
SEARCH t USING INDEX idx_lower (<expr>=?)
```

### The covering index

If the index contains every column the query needs, the engine can answer from the index
alone and never touch the table:

```sql
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM t WHERE name > 'name1';
```

```
SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX idx_name (name>?)
```

**COVERING** is the word to look for. It means the second lookup — index to row — didn't
happen at all, and it's why adding one more column to an index sometimes makes a query
several times faster than adding a whole new index would.

### Worth knowing: LIKE 'x%' does not use your index, and the reason is a default

A prefix search looks like it should be an index range scan: everything starting with
`name7` is contiguous in a sorted list. Try it:

```sql
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM t WHERE name LIKE 'name7%';
```

```
SCAN t
```

The reason is that SQLite's `LIKE` is **case-insensitive for ASCII by default**, while
your index is sorted case-sensitively (BINARY collation). Sorted by `A < a < b`, an
index cannot produce the range "everything matching `name7` in either case" as one
contiguous run — so the optimiser correctly refuses.

Two ways out, and both restore the range scan:

```sql
PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON;
CREATE INDEX idx_ci ON t(name COLLATE NOCASE);
```

Either makes the collation of the question match the collation of the index, and the
plan turns into `SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX ... (name>? AND name<?)` — note that it
became a *range*, `>` and `<`, which is exactly what a prefix match is once you can
trust the order.

The general lesson outlives SQLite: **an index is only usable by a query whose collation
matches the index's.** In PostgreSQL this is the same trap wearing different clothes —
a `LIKE 'x%'` index scan there requires either the C locale or an explicit
`text_pattern_ops` index, and thousands of people have discovered that on production the
week after it worked locally.

quiz.prompt: You add an index to speed up a slow report. Name two costs you have just taken on.

options.text: The table has to be locked while the index exists
options.why: Building an index takes a lock briefly, but having one doesn't. If it did, nobody would use indexes.

options.text: Every write to the table now maintains a second tree, and the database grows
options.why: An index is a real sorted copy of real data. Inserts and updates of the indexed column write both trees, and the copy occupies real pages — sometimes more than the table itself.

options.text: Existing queries must be rewritten to reference the index by name
options.why: The optimiser picks indexes; queries name tables and columns. Being able to add an index without touching query text is most of the point.

options.text: Reads of other columns get slower
options.why: Unindexed reads are unaffected. The optimiser simply won't use the index for them; it doesn't get in the way.

quiz.prompt: A query filtering on an indexed column shows `SCAN` in its plan. Give two different reasons that can happen even though the index exists and the column is right.

options.text: The column is wrapped in a function, or the query's collation doesn't match the index's
options.why: Both break the same rule: an index answers questions about the exact value in the exact order it was sorted. `lower(col)` is a different value; a case-insensitive `LIKE` against a case-sensitive index is a different order.

options.text: SELECT * always forces a scan
options.why: `SELECT *` prevents an index being *covering*, so the engine must fetch rows after the index lookup. It doesn't stop the lookup happening.

options.text: The index is too new for the optimiser to have noticed it
options.why: Indexes are visible to the planner as soon as they're created. Stale *statistics* can cause bad estimates, but that's a different failure and it doesn't hide the index.

options.text: The table is too small, so the optimiser refuses to use any index
options.why: A tempting answer, because on a tiny table a scan genuinely can be cheaper and the optimiser may choose it. But that's the optimiser being right, not the index being unusable — and it isn't one of the two structural reasons.

quiz.prompt: What does `COVERING` mean in a query plan, and what work does it save?

options.text: The index covers every row in the table, so no rows can be missed
options.why: Ordinary indexes always contain every row (partial indexes aside). "Covering" is about columns, not rows.

options.text: The engine has locked the rows the index points at
options.why: Nothing to do with locking. A covering read touches fewer things, if anything.

options.text: The index is large enough to be held entirely in memory
options.why: Caching is real and helps, but it's not what the word means and it isn't what the plan is reporting.

options.text: The index holds every column the query needs, so the engine answers from the index and never reads the table
options.why: It eliminates the second hop — index entry to actual row — which on a large table is a random page read per matching row, and usually dominates the cost.

quiz.prompt: Your table has an index on `email`. Which of these can use it — `WHERE email = ?`, `WHERE lower(email) = ?`, `WHERE email LIKE 'a%'`?

options.text: Only the first; the other two can never use an index
options.why: Both are recoverable: an expression index handles `lower(email)`, and a matching collation handles the prefix match.

options.text: All three, since all three filter on the indexed column
options.why: Naming the column isn't enough — the index stores one specific value in one specific order, and two of these ask about something else.

options.text: The first and second; `LIKE` can never use an index
options.why: Backwards on both counts. `lower(email)` needs an expression index, while a *prefix* `LIKE` is genuinely index-friendly given the right collation. A leading `%` is the one that can't be helped.

options.text: The first straight away; the second not at all; the third only if the index's collation matches how LIKE compares
options.why: Equality on the bare column is exactly what the index is sorted for. `lower(email)` is a value the index doesn't contain. The prefix match is a range scan in principle, but only once the question's collation and the index's agree.

quiz.prompt: Why does an index make `ORDER BY name` cheaper even for a query that returns every row in the table?

options.text: The index lets the engine skip rows it doesn't need
options.why: This query needs every row. The saving is the ordering, not any filtering.

options.text: Sorting happens in memory either way, so it's the same cost
options.why: Only if it fits. A sort too big for the buffer spills to disk, which is exactly the cost the ordered index avoids.

options.text: The index is already stored in that order, so there is nothing to sort
options.why: Sorted order is the index's entire nature. Reading it in order yields rows in order, turning a sort into a walk — no temporary file, no sort buffer.

options.text: It doesn't — returning every row means a scan, so the index is unused
options.why: A full read still has to produce the requested order somehow. Doing it by reading a pre-sorted structure beats sorting the whole table.

task.markdown:
Prove each of these to yourself rather than taking the lesson's word for it. Use a table
with a few hundred rows — small is fine, the plan doesn't depend on size here.

1. Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for an equality filter with no index. Record the plan.
2. Add the index, run it again, and record how the plan changed.
3. Wrap the column in `lower()` and watch it fall back to a scan.
4. Add an expression index and watch it recover.
5. Get one query to report `COVERING INDEX`, and work out why that one qualifies when
   your earlier one didn't.
6. Reproduce the `LIKE 'x%'` scan, then fix it with a `COLLATE NOCASE` index and confirm
   the plan turns into a range.

Write every plan you saw into the file as a comment beside the query that produced it.
That file is the point of the exercise, not the queries.
checklist: the same query planned both with and without an index, both plans recorded
a function on the indexed column observed falling back to `SCAN`
an expression index built, and the plan recovering
one query reporting `COVERING INDEX`, and you can say why
`LIKE 'x%'` scanning, then using a range after the collation is fixed

days.title: NULL is not a value
days.teaser: The query that returned zero rows for two years and never logged an error
days.teachBack: Walk through why `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` returns nothing for every possible `x`. Expand the expression, say what each term evaluates to, and explain why `WHERE` then drops the row.
days.theoryMarkdown:
The last two days were physical. This one is about semantics, and it's here early
because it is the single most reliable source of quietly wrong answers in SQL — the kind
that don't error, don't look odd, and are off by exactly the rows you cared about.

### Three-valued logic

Most languages have two truth values. SQL has three: **true, false, and unknown**.

`NULL` does not mean zero, or empty string, or "false". It means *no value is recorded
here*, and the consequence is that any comparison involving it can't produce a verdict:

```sql
SELECT NULL = NULL;
SELECT NULL <> NULL;
SELECT NULL IS NULL;
```

The first two return `NULL` — not true, not false. Only the third returns `1`. That is
the whole design in three lines: **you cannot ask whether an unknown equals anything,
including another unknown.** "Is the value I don't know the same as the other value I
don't know?" has no honest answer but "unknown", and SQL refuses to invent one.

`WHERE` keeps only rows where the condition is **true**. Unknown is not true, so:

```sql
SELECT 1 WHERE NULL = NULL;
```

returns no rows. Not an error, not a warning — silence. That silence is the entire
problem.

### The one that has actually cost people money

`NOT IN` with a `NULL` anywhere in the list returns nothing. Ever.

```sql
SELECT 3 WHERE 3 IN (1, NULL);
SELECT 3 WHERE 3 NOT IN (1, NULL);
```

Both come back empty, and the second is the dangerous one. Expand it: `3 NOT IN (1,
NULL)` is `3 <> 1 AND 3 <> NULL`, which is `true AND unknown`, which is **unknown** —
not true, so the row is dropped. It doesn't matter that 3 obviously isn't in the list.
As long as one `NULL` is present, `NOT IN` can never return true for any value.

The usual shape in real code:

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM banned_customers);
```

The day someone inserts a `banned_customers` row with a `NULL` id, this query silently
returns zero orders. It has been correct for two years; nothing was deployed; there is
no error in any log. Use `NOT EXISTS` instead, which asks a row-at-a-time question and
is immune:

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders o
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM banned_customers b WHERE b.id = o.customer_id);
```

### Aggregates quietly disagree with each other

```sql
CREATE TABLE u(v INTEGER);
INSERT INTO u VALUES (1), (2), (NULL);
SELECT count(*), count(v), sum(v), avg(v) FROM u;
```

`3, 2, 3, 1.5`.

`count(*)` counts rows. `count(v)` counts **non-null values** — a different question with
a confusingly similar spelling. `sum` and `avg` skip nulls entirely, so the average is
3/2, not 3/3. If your "average response time" quietly excludes every request that
timed out and recorded no time, you have a metric that improves as your service gets
worse.

### Where NULL suddenly does equal NULL

Having insisted that nothing equals `NULL`, SQL then has two places where nulls are
treated as the same thing after all:

```sql
SELECT v, count(*) FROM u GROUP BY v;
```

`GROUP BY` puts all the nulls in one group, and `DISTINCT` collapses them to one row.
It has to — grouping is about identity, not comparison — but it does mean the same
`NULL` that refuses to equal itself in a `WHERE` cheerfully groups with itself one clause
later.

### Worth knowing: UNIQUE doesn't mean unique

```sql
CREATE TABLE w(v INTEGER UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO w VALUES (NULL), (NULL), (NULL);
SELECT count(*) FROM w;
```

Three rows, no error. A `UNIQUE` constraint is enforced by comparing values, and two
nulls don't compare equal, so the constraint has nothing to object to. Standard SQL
requires this, and SQLite, PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL all agree.

This is why "one active session per user" implemented as a nullable `UNIQUE` column
lets you create unlimited sessions with a null in it. PostgreSQL 15 finally added
`UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` to opt out — a good clue as to how often this bites, since
it took the standard about forty years to admit people wanted the other behaviour.

quiz.prompt: `SELECT NULL = NULL` — what comes back, and why isn't it either true or false?

options.text: An error — nulls can't be compared with `=`
options.why: It's perfectly legal SQL and runs silently. The silence is what makes null bugs hard to find.

options.text: `1`, because a null is equal to itself like any other value
options.why: That's the intuition the design deliberately rejects. `NULL` marks an absent value, and two absences aren't evidence of sameness. `IS NULL` is the operator that returns 1 here.

options.text: `0`, because a null isn't equal to anything
options.why: Close, and a common half-memory — but false would be a verdict, and the engine isn't entitled to one. Unknown is not the same as false, which is exactly why `NOT` can't rescue it.

options.text: `NULL`, because comparing two unknowns can't produce a verdict
options.why: SQL has three truth values. "Is the value I don't know equal to the other value I don't know?" has no honest answer, so the comparison yields unknown rather than inventing one.

quiz.prompt: Why does `WHERE x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` return no rows regardless of what `x` is?

options.text: `NOT IN` doesn't accept null values in its list and returns empty
options.why: The null is accepted quite happily. The emptiness comes from three-valued logic, not from a rejection.

options.text: The optimiser can't build a plan, so it returns nothing
options.why: The plan is fine and the query runs normally. The result is the honest consequence of the logic, not a planner failure.

options.text: It returns no rows only when `x` is itself null
options.why: It returns nothing for every `x`, null or not — including values obviously not in the list, which is what makes it so hard to spot.

options.text: It expands to `x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL`, and that last term is unknown, so the whole condition is never true
options.why: `true AND unknown` is unknown, and `WHERE` keeps only rows where the condition is true. One null in the list is enough to make the answer unknown for every row.

quiz.prompt: A table has 100 rows; 30 have a null `duration`. What do `count(*)`, `count(duration)` and `avg(duration)` report, and which silently misleads?

options.text: 100, 70, and the mean of the 70 non-null values — the average, because it quietly excludes the missing ones
options.why: `avg` divides by the count of non-null values, not by the number of rows. If nulls are your timeouts, the average improves as the service gets worse.

options.text: 100, 70, and null, since any null in the input poisons the aggregate
options.why: That's true of arithmetic on nulls (`1 + NULL` is null) but not of aggregates. Aggregates skip nulls and return a real number — which is precisely why the problem is invisible.

options.text: 100, 100 and the mean over all 100 rows, treating nulls as zero
options.why: Nothing in SQL treats a null as zero. Both `count(col)` and `avg` skip them entirely.

options.text: All three report 70, since nulls aren't really rows
options.why: `count(*)` counts rows and doesn't look at values at all, so it reports 100. The gap between it and `count(col)` is the tell.

quiz.prompt: Name the two places where SQL treats two nulls as the same thing, despite `NULL = NULL` being unknown.

options.text: `JOIN ... ON` and `UNIQUE` constraints
options.why: Both go the other way: a join on null columns matches nothing, and `UNIQUE` permits many nulls precisely because it can't call them equal.

options.text: `COUNT` and `SUM`
options.why: Those skip nulls rather than grouping them. Skipping is a third behaviour again — neither equal nor unequal, just absent.

options.text: `GROUP BY` puts them in one group, and `DISTINCT` collapses them to one row
options.why: Both are about identity rather than comparison, so they have to make a choice — and they choose to treat nulls as one thing. The same null that won't equal itself in a `WHERE` groups with itself a clause later.

options.text: `ORDER BY` and `WHERE`
options.why: `ORDER BY` gives nulls a consistent *position*, which isn't the same as calling them equal, and `WHERE` is the clause where a null comparison drops the row.

quiz.prompt: You add `UNIQUE` to a nullable column to enforce "at most one active session per user". What actually happens?

options.text: Rows with a null in that column are all allowed, because two nulls never compare equal
options.why: The constraint is enforced by comparison, and nulls don't compare equal, so it has nothing to object to. You get unlimited rows with a null there — the standard requires this, and every major engine complies.

options.text: It works, since only one row can be active at a time anyway
options.why: Nothing enforces that. The whole point is that the constraint you added does not constrain the case you cared about.

options.text: The second null insert is rejected, like any duplicate
options.why: That's the intuition the constraint doesn't share. PostgreSQL 15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` specifically to offer this behaviour as an opt-in.

options.text: The column is implicitly made `NOT NULL`
options.why: `UNIQUE` and `NOT NULL` are independent. If you want both, you have to say both.

task.markdown:
Make each of these bite, then fix it.

1. Build a small table with some nulls in it.
2. Write a `NOT IN` query against a subquery that contains a null, and confirm it returns
   nothing when it obviously should return rows.
3. Rewrite the same question with `NOT EXISTS` and confirm it's now correct.
4. Show `count(*)`, `count(col)`, `sum` and `avg` disagreeing on the same column, and
   work out by hand what the average *should* be if nulls counted as zero.
5. Create a `UNIQUE` column and insert three nulls into it. Then find a way to actually
   forbid that — a partial index or a `CHECK` will do it.
checklist: `NULL = NULL` evaluated, and the result is neither 0 nor 1
a `NOT IN` query returning nothing because of one null, demonstrated
the same question answered correctly with `NOT EXISTS`
three nulls inserted into a `UNIQUE` column, then a constraint that does stop them
